idiom_name: function component with useState/useReducer/useSyncExternalStore rendering stateless children
implementation_notes: The modern container is an ordinary function component: it owns state with useState or useReducer, subscribes to external sources with useSyncExternalStore, runs effects in useEffect, and renders children that receive nothing but props. Because hooks can be extracted, the wrapper is optional - a custom hook plus a presentational component separates logic from view in one file less - so reach for the container when the state source must be injectable (tests, previews, a mocked store) or when the wrapper is the routing/data-loading boundary. Children must stay renderable from a literal props object.
pitfalls: The snapshot returned by getSnapshot must be immutable and remain identical while the store is unchanged, otherwise the component re-renders in a loop or shows stale data.
An effect that subscribes must return its cleanup; a listener left behind keeps the component and its store alive after unmount.
Copying a prop into the child's useState freezes the child on the first value - keep it controlled and drive it from props.

variants.name: Class container (React.Component)
variants.idiom_name: class extending React.Component with this.state and lifecycle subscriptions
variants.implementation_notes: The original container is a class: state is assigned once in the constructor (never through setState there), updates go through setState, subscriptions are opened in componentDidMount and closed in componentWillUnmount, and render() stays pure - it is called on every update and may only consult this.props and this.state. Use this form when maintaining an older codebase, for error boundaries, or when getSnapshotBeforeUpdate is genuinely needed; otherwise the hook container is the current default. The 2019 update to the original article notes hooks make the split optional, which is why the class form is no longer the recommendation.
pitfalls: setState is asynchronous and batched, so reading this.state right after calling it returns the old value; use the updater form or derive from the previous state.
Copying props into state (this.state = { color: props.color }) freezes the value and ignores later prop updates.
Assigning this.state outside the constructor, or calling setState in the constructor, leaves render() with unexpected state - initialise directly in the constructor instead.
